There seems to be a correlation between this particular problem and large collections of related objects, but it's hard to be more specific or definitive.  I suspect it will not be very useful to test by creating a bunch of independent objects and versioning them – at least that's not what our repository looks like.  It's a large set of interrelated object many of which have large files attached to them, etc., etc.  FWIW we did a fair amount of testing of our repository migration process, but only with a little over 10,000 objects; in production we have well over 300,000 objects.
Are the versioned resources that exhibit this error still usable? If not, than that would make this a blocker, and we would want to include it in a 4.5.2 release. Thoughts?
Yes, we do see this issue as a blocker.
Are the versioned resources that exhibit this error still usable?

We do have examples of objects that exhibit this problem which also appear to have other problems, at least insofar as ActiveFedora is concerned.  In one case of note, I am not able to create a new relationship from an object to this "damaged" object – i.e., where the damaged object is the object of an RDF triple.  I have not tried a raw SPARQL update directly to Fedora, but strangely we not seeing errors, just a silent failure of the operation.

the reasons I thought they were related were that both seemed to be version creation errors (that I think Andrew had narrowed down to a race condition on isFrozen), and that in those PUT 404s talk we were having you linked me a stacktrace that suggested that a similar node that didn't exist:
https://gist.github.com/dchandekstark/40245ba9a3d02dedebfdc9f32c7e069e

versionManager:179

In the meantime, we will hold off on a 4.5.2 release.

Here's what I'd try to do to debug it:
1.  Eliminate the possibility that there's a critical bug in fedora when dealing with your example data.

It wouldn't surprise me if certain version labels were invalid, or if other characteristics of the resources being versionioned might result in an exception.  It's relatively easy to test this if you're doing a migration.  Simply perform the migration of that problematic object against a clean repository.  If it works fine, great, we can dig a little deeper.
2.  Try to find a pattern in the errors.
This is trickier.  Some odd possibilities that come to mind are:

a) There's a small amount of corrupted entries, but they have sha1s that match "new" content you're versioning:  since modeshape doesn't actually persist new content if it already has a node with the given sha1, a corruption or problem in the database might show up in seemingly unrelated places.  For example if in a fedora 3 migration a lot of versions of datastreams are identical (perhaps there's an empty template for a MODS record, or DC record or something) and for some reason the fedora 4 database has corruption on that record, whenever you try to access that content again you'd get an error.

b) I don't have any other ideas for now, but if you can get errors consistently (though unpredictably) maybe export each resource before you make the version snapshot, then if you get an error snapshotting you'll have a copy of the resource that triggered the problem.  You wouldn't have to retain the exports if the version operation is successful.

https://github.com/fcrepo4/fcrepo4/blob/fcrepo-4.5.1/fcrepo-kernel-modeshape/src/main/java/org/fcrepo/kernel/modeshape/services/VersionServiceImpl.java#L177

The VersionHistory for that resource appears to be in an invalid state. That being the case, the likely resolution is to clear the invalid history. We could 1) add logic to auto-remove the VersionHistory when this exception is caught, or 2) you can delete and re-ingest the resource.
Thoughts,
Ideally, we could find an association between the errors you reported during ingest:
https://jira.duraspace.org/browse/FCREPO-2053
..and the resources that have invalid histories. If we knew under which circumstances the version state becomes invalid, we could prevent it from happening in the first place.
How would you like to proceed?

If I understand options #1 and #2 above – namely, if a version history becomes corrupted, to either wipe the version history or delete and re-ingest – then neither seems acceptable, at least in the long run.  If this were a very rare occurrence or edge case that choice might be tolerable; I can't see it at the error rate we are currently experiencing in the apparent absence of any other known problem.  So, it seems that we need to root out the underlying conditions of the corruption.  I suppose it is possible that

is somehow related, but my sense was that that issue was more likely a side effect of delays/timeouts caused by the long-running delete query which appears to have been fixed by indexing the timestamp (version) column.
I agree that rooting out the originating source of the invalid VersionHistory would be an effect next step.
Are there commonalities between the affected resources?
Are there previous errors or warnings in the Fedora log related to the affected resources?
Can we reproduce the conditions for new resources?

One commonality that we have noted is that the problem seems to arise when versioning all the objects in a particular collection (and, in particular, a large collection) and, when it does arise, it seems to follow a common pattern.  For example, yesterday, we queued up version creation jobs for a collection containing something over 12,000 objects.  The first 4500 or so jobs proceeded with no failures.  Then, the jobs began failing.  Once the jobs began failing, all the subsequent queued up jobs also failed.  At one point we stopped the job queue, stopped and restarted Tomcat, and resumed the job queue.  The remaining queued up jobs immediately continued failing.  This pattern seems to be – running a batch of version creation jobs for smaller collections (say, 6500 objects or less) seems to succeed and running a batch of version creation jobs for larger collections seems to work for some number of objects in that collection and then start failing.
Also, note that all the objects in a collection have a relationship to the collection object – don't know if that is a factor or not.
Adding to
's comment above, FWIW all objects in a collection have a <
http://projecthydra.org/ns/relations#isGovernedBy
> rel to the collection.  The immediate "descendants" of a collection also have a <info:fedora/fedora-system:def/relations-external#isMemberOfCollection> rel to the collection.

I suspect you are using Hydra machinery for this, but describing what is happening at the Fedora-level would be helpful. Details on the concurrency of this process would also be instructive.
As a side note, have you tried throttling your versioning jobs?

If the collection-versioning process involves updating the parent collection, invalidation of the collection's version history could potentially explain why after a certain point all subsequent versioning requests fail.
If you can provide specifics of how you version collections, we can work from there. Thanks!
